question: My Manitoba Hydro electricity bill says the latest meter reading was 'estimated.' Does that mean a reader physically visited my meter, and what can I check?
generated_answer:
You may not be aware that Manitoba Hydro's meter readers have been visiting your home or business for years. You may not have been home to see them. The term 'estimated' is used when a reader is unable to access the meter for a reading. The next time a reader is able to access your meter, they will take a reading and compare it to the estimated amount on your bill. Any difference in the amounts will be corrected and you'll be billed accordingly. If you're concerned about the accuracy of your bill, you can read your meter yourself and compare it to the reading shown on your bill. If the reading you took differs from what's on your bill, please call us at 204-360-3117. We'll be happy to help. Where is my meter? Your electricity meter is usually located in a meter box, sometimes called a meter pit, in the front of your home or business. The boxes are typically located at ground level, and you may have to move some brushes or debris to access the meter. Please take care when clearing your meter pit. There may be other wires or cables in the pit that could pose a safety hazard. What do I need to know when reading my meter? Your electricity meter tells Manitoba Hydro how much electricity you are using. The actual amount may be more or less than what you paid for. The display on your meter may look like one of the following:

A seven-segment display

If you have a meter with a seven-segment display, you'll see a row of single numbers, reading across from left to right. To take your meter reading, simply read the numbers from left to right, including the numbers in the decimal point. For example, the meter reading shown below is 61924

A five/6 digit display

If you have a meter with a five or six digit display, you'll see a row of numbers across your meter. To take your meter reading, simply read the numbers from left to right, including the numbers in the decimal point. For example, the meter reading shown below is 61924.2

A digital meter

If you have a digital meter, you'll see a seven-segment digital display. To take your meter reading, simply read the numbers from left to right, including the numbers in the decimal point. For example, the meter reading shown below is 12024.6

What do the different numbers on my meter mean? The numbers on your meter represent the amount of electricity you've used in kilowatt hours (kWh). The numbers on the meter may be rolling over, which means they are getting close to their limit. When the numbers roll over, the meter starts over again at zero. Don't be alarmed if you see that your meter reading is higher than what you paid for. This is because Manitoba Hydro bills you for the amount of electricity you've used, not the amount that's displayed on your meter. If you're concerned about the accuracy of your bill, you can read your meter yourself and compare it to the reading shown on your bill. If the reading you took differs from what's on your bill, please call us at 204-360-3117. We'll be happy to help. What is the difference between the 'current reading' and 'previous reading' on my bill? The 'current reading' is the amount of electricity you've used up to the date of your bill. The 'previous reading' is the amount of electricity you used during your previous billing period. The difference between the two readings represents the amount of electricity you've used during the current billing period. Why is my bill higher than normal? - Increased usage due to the weather. If it's been a particularly hot summer or a cold winter, you may have used more electricity to heat or cool your home.

- New appliances or electronics. If you've recently purchased a new appliance or electronic device, it may be using more electricity than you're used to.

- Changes in your household. If you've had a change in your household, such as a new baby or a family member moving in, you may be using more electricity than usual.

- Meter reading errors. It's possible that the meter reader made an error when taking your meter reading, resulting in a higher bill.
